description: Angeline Stickney, a young woman from the Amber Adirondack River region, attended college despite low women’s wages and societal prejudice, relying on frugality and her mother’s moral support. She was determined to pursue education, influenced by her sister Ruth, who lacked her indomitable will and ultimately did not attend college due to poor health and the unavailability of student fare. Ruth, though unable to attend, provided financial help and emotional support, writing to Angeline about her loneliness and desire to share emotions. Angeline’s college experience included four male classmates, whom she regarded as noble, and she faced a breakdown six weeks before graduation due to exhaustion. Monochromatic painting and tissue-paper flowers were considered as alternatives to college but offered minimal experience. Angeline desired both her own and her sister’s education, justifying her ambition through her sister’s advancement. Ruth returned to McGrawville in 1854, stayed briefly, and later supported Angeline’s journey.

A woman of gentle voice, iron will, and utmost purity of character instilled moral principles in her sons through leadership and self-sacrifice, organizing them to perform household tasks like sweeping, dusting, and mending fences, while allowing leisure in swimming and skating. She served as their school teacher, teaching the three R’s and other subjects. A fourteen-year-old girl wrote to Mr. George Waldo about the Sugar Maple tree, noting its sap yields sugar used for cooking, furniture, and warmth, and its ashes produce potash, which with flint and sand makes glass. Glass enables the elderly to see and provides light to homes, and telescopes made of glass allow discovery of planetary knowledge. Angeline Hall worked for Professor Kingley, receiving board and performing chores like washing dishes and sweeping, and remained in contact with her sister Ruth. Asaph Hall made a prism of glass filled with water, a tool used in scientific observation.

The speaker has stabilized the home situation, making it clean and comfortable despite its unstable old brick and mortar structure, which fails under wind, open windows, or slamming doors. The home is described as a place where people are bound by a master link—symbolized by Mrs. John R. Eastman, whose steady, calm voice through open windows provided spiritual warmth and connection. Angeline Hall, a central figure, emphasized absolute truth and Christian principles, demanding honesty in word and deed, and her influence shaped the family’s moral life, though her strict views caused personal hardship for the speaker. Mr. Hall focused on astronomy, contributing to the world’s gain of a worthy astronomer, while Mrs. Hall dedicated herself to domestic care, yielding a devoted wife and mother. The speaker feels like a stranger in a strange land, believing home is where the other person is, and expresses a desire for quiet strength in a small room. The world gained a scientist and a devoted mother, possibly losing a reformer-poetess.

Angeline Hall, a daughter of the pioneers, was a devout Unitarian who rejected church traditions and superstition, seeking a faith grounded in scientific truth and moral integrity. She valued education deeply, influenced by her grandmother, a Harvard graduate who sent her four sons to Harvard College. Angeline raised her four sons with firmness and gentleness, making obedience to her word a sacred duty. Despite her frailty and lack of time for travel or charity, she remained devoted to her husband, whose intellectual pursuits she admired and supported. Her story is compared to a romance and argues that college-educated women should marry men earning at least one dollar per day—excluding European nobility but favoring American nobility. The family moved east after a storm barred West from Lake Erie; fifty years later, all four sons graduated from Harvard, a rare achievement that astonished observers who saw her collapse at McGrawville. She passed her final days in Virginia, longed to visit Europe, and on Christmas Day 1891, shared a meal with her husband and sons at Georgetown.

Angeline Hall lived in Georgetown, where she raised her four sons and owned the home at No. 18 Gay Street for 25 years. She made her I Street home cheerful, hosting birthday feasts, but it was invaded by smallpox, which Captain Fox contracted while boarding with the Halls; Mr. Hall’s sister caught the disease but recovered without spreading it. Oscar Fox and Colonel A. J. Warner, college friends of Angeline, fought in the battles of Bull Run and Antietam, with Warner surviving a hip wound due to successful surgery. Mrs. Hall supported George W. Hill, encouraging his appointment to the U.S. Navy’s Corps of Professors of Mathematics after he passed a competitive examination. She served as directress of the tenth, eleventh, and twelfth wards and was active in a benevolent society in Georgetown. The Halls formed close friendships with quiet individuals, including Dr. Morrill Wyman, their physician. Their second child, Samuel, was born in 1864 at Gunbarrel Corner.

Asaph Hall 3rd, born October 15, 1829, was the eldest of six children and spent his early years in easy circumstances, developing a taste for literature. His physical development was shaped by his mother, widow Hannah (Palmer) Hall, and he began serious study at age 24 or 25, bringing vigor from an unspoiled youth and mature strength. He studied astronomy under Brünnow and French, earning admiration from peers and encouragement from teachers. He read Gauss’s Theoria Motus in 1858 and learned German through his wife, Angeline Stickney. Angeline, a student at N.Y. Central College, embraced the institution’s ideals, became a woman suffragist, and adopted the bloomers. Cupid arranged for the young man to take a geometry course with Miss Stickney, where he asked hard questions to embarrass her, but instead earned admiration. The couple lived near the observatory in Cambridge, and their marriage faced challenges due to Angeline’s feeble health, though her mental strength was exceptional.

New York Central College, located in McGrawville, Cortland County, was a reformist and abolitionist institution open to all regardless of race or gender, supported by John Pierpont, Gerrit Smith, and Horace Greeley. It had about ninety students in 1852, focused on political and social reforms, and emphasized declamation, debate, and oratory. Angeline Stickney, a student, completed her curriculum there, taught mathematics, and was known for her perfect academic standing and moral conduct. She expressed deep love and spiritual connection with Asaph Hall, believing God sent him to her, and hoped their love would bring harmony and good to others. In philosophical terms, light corresponds to knowledge and unveils all things, while love corresponds to gravitation, bringing harmony and enabling humans to fill heaven and themselves with heaven. Love, through self-forgetfulness and tender service, wears out the silver cord, leading to a seraphic, luminous spiritual beauty. The college produced many patriotic individuals and was a precursor to Cornell University.

The father is a central figure who visits Mr. Kings and the museum with the narrator and Sam., and is seen by Dr. Peters in New York. He is with Sam. and C. A. S. Hall during tea and is associated with Asaph Jr., who will go ahead of him if he maintains good health. The narrator walks through swamp and woods in the rain to visit Sister Ruth, climbing a hill as high as any in McGrawville from which they see a fine prospect. Flowers bloom on hill and plain in dull soil, producing haunting perfume or heavenly stain, symbolizing aspiration. Poetry, especially in the works of Angeline Stickney and C. A. S. Hall, reflects inner longing and spiritual aspiration, with themes of freedom, worship, and the human soul. Sam. is translating Aeschylus and reading Goethe’s Faust aloud, while working on Prometheus Unbound with a personal plan and determination. The narrator longs for a quiet room to write and study, and one of their earliest memories is seeing a red infant in the father’s hands. The Historical Society begins work the day after Thanksgiving.

The house stood on a knoll with a view of Lake Ontario, near a deep ravine known as Rodman’s gulf, a field of round boulders where the sisters played house, and woods across the road where they gathered hemlock knots for their mother. The sisters, including Angeline and Elmina, were inseparable and learned self-reliance from their motherless upbringing, with Grandfather Cook providing protection and kindness half a mile up the road. He drove sixty miles for salt and took the family on religious drives. David, a man known as the "sweet singer of Rodman," lived nearby, and Elmina was won by him. In 1864, during the Civil War, the house was threatened by Confederate forces, prompting a move to a hiding place in the Rock Creek valley. In 1876, the house was enlarged to three stories with a flat tin roof and bay windows. The sisters found joy in nature, including wild berries and flowers, and the writer admired two individuals for their intellectual and imaginative traits. Aunt Ruth reported David’s laziness and the deaths of neighbors, and the speaker sent her thirty dollars.

Chloe Angeline Stickney, born in Rodman, New York, on All Saints’ Day, 1830, is the sixth child of a carpenter, with three older sisters and two younger brothers who died in infancy. Her mother, Mrs. Hall, became head of the Stickney family after her death in 1878. Chloe’s birthday influenced her ideals, and she later told her sons it fell on All Saints’ Day. The young carpenter, A. Hall, hesitated to marry Angeline Stickney, a sincere Baptist who joined the church at sixteen, though she remembered a suitor from McGrawville whose love was slow and bashful. Hall, who proved himself more than a carpenter after completing a house for a neighbor with perfect timbers, later resolved to become an architect. After losing his home and farm of eighty-five acres due to unpaid work, he moved his family to the Genesee Country. Asaph Hall, a carpenter who became an astronomer, is noted as an example of impecunious Americans from excellent families.

Mrs. Hall provided her family with food through skilled cooking, canning abundant fruit for winter, and serving plain, wholesome meals centered on Virginia beef and mutton from Georgetown markets, banning pork and lard in favor of beef suet. She maintained strict economy, kept the house clean from roof to cellar, mended clothing, and extended aid to the poor, requiring only one servant whom she taught her sons to assist. Mr. Hall objected to living in Washington, preferring New England due to the city’s overcrowding, disease, and moral decay, including forty smallpox cases and immoral women who jeered at Union soldiers. Sister Ruth was intensely religious, considered a saving grace, and taught in an adjoining district; she was seen often by a scholar in 1952 who studied in winter with limited opportunity. The women had a strong appetite for whiskey, bartering butter for liquor, and one took little Asaph to a saloon where he was found with the servant joking with rough men. Mr. Spear was consistently present at prayer meetings, offering beautiful and instructive words, and the Savior was believed to bless and strengthen people.

The narrator, seeking to establish a painting class, visited multiple locations including Felts Mills, the Great Bend, and the Academy, where Mr. Clark displayed the narrator’s paintings. On Monday, Jan. 12th, the narrator decided not to stay at Felts Mills due to only three scholars showing interest. Miss Wright and others expressed interest in painting lessons, leading the narrator to find a boarding place at Mr. Horr’s, who hosted seven boarders, two daughters, a hired girl, and an adopted child. The narrator taught Miss Goddard and Miss Wright in painting, and on Thursday, Jan. 14th, despite stormy weather, attended the Academy meeting. Mr. Horr hosted the narrator and later, on March 4th, Frederick brought Horr to Philadelphia, where Horr hoped to form a class in flowers. The narrator eventually left Gouverneur with $15, having tried to form a class without success, and later traveled to North Wilna, where he reflected on past experiences and the quiet, feminine household of Angeline Stickney. Rain and storms frequently interrupted efforts to form classes.

Professor Hall, a scholar and writer, is the central figure, known for authoring the introduction to "Observations and Orbits of the Satellites of Mars," where he describes how the favorable opposition of Mars in the spring of 1877 inspired his use of the Clark refractor to search for a satellite. He has sisters Adelaide and Adeline, and Mary Humphrey, who is seen by the boys and is a sister of Professor Hall. A. (likely Asaph Hall) meets the writer at the depot in New Haven, stays with him, and drives him to East Rock, which overlooks the city, sea, and surrounding country. A. Jr. has poor health and is advised to come up to stay with the writer’s family. Angeline Hall is feeling well but warns of a possible mild malarial fever and asks to be written to soon. The writer stayed near college buildings on Wall Street, did not reach the Observatory until Sunday afternoon, and visited various locations including Prof. Wrights’ lab, the Insurance Building, and Mrs. Winchesters’ greenhouses. A. held a smoke-talk on Saturdays that inspired a country boy to become a civil engineer.

The young astronomer, residing in Boston in 1858, attended Music Hall meetings where speakers like Wendell Phillips, Garrison, and Theodore Parker delivered impassioned speeches; Phillips, after Lincoln’s election, advocated disunion, leading to threats of mobbing and a body-guard being formed, which included Asaph Hall, who recalled Phillips’ calm demeanor and courteous bow. The astronomer earned one dollar per moon-culmination observation, making twenty-three in March 1858, and later began computing almanacs, earning about $130 annually before competition reduced profitability. In early 1859, after the death of elder Bond, his salary rose to $400, which he considered generous. His wife regularly wakened him and sent him to the observatory. Asaph Hall, a six-foot-tall man who believed in fair play, was treated poorly due to poverty and was eventually assisted by Deacon Holmes in Cambridgeport. Hall’s work on a comet’s orbit was published in the Astronomical Journal, earning him a friendship with editor Dr. B. A. Gould and an associate role in the National Academy of Sciences.

Asaph Hall, an astronomer elevated to prominence during the Civil War, worked at the U.S. Naval Observatory starting in the summer of 1862, becoming an "Aid" after passing an examination. He faced government inefficiency and political interference, criticizing "American astronomy" at the observatory, yet contributed positively to American astronomy. His wife, Angeline Hall, supported him emotionally and intellectually, encouraging his work, supplying him with nourishing meals, and awaiting results with eager interest. She believed in a well-rounded life for women, advocating for the American woman to match Spartan, Roman, or modern European ideals as a devoted wife and mother. During the Civil War, she helped distribute supplies to Black residents in Washington and later visited a Home for Destitute <DW52> Women and Children. Miss Sarah Waitt, a Cambridge schoolteacher and friend, noted the happiness of Mr. and Mrs. Hall’s marriage. Hall’s wife also wrote to Captain Gillis, urging a fair selection process based on ability, not influence. One night, Abraham Lincoln visited the observatory, asking about an inverted moon. Hall’s work and personal life were shaped by mutual support, resilience, and a commitment to both science and social duty.

A two-story brick house with white stucco and a shingled roof stood in a generous yard, facing southward, and featured a front porch with wooden pillars. The house included a hall with a parlor and sitting room, the dining room behind the sitting room, and a room over the sitting room where Mrs. Hall sat in an oak rocking chair to do family sewing—this space was of equal importance to the dining room and sitting room. Open coal fires with grates were in both the dining and sitting rooms, which were connected by sliding doors and served as the center of home comfort. The family, including Angeline, gathered at the fireside to worship and give thanks, though Angeline was frightened by stories and had a weak stomach, vomiting after eating salt pork. Asaph Hall, a skilled carpenter from Connecticut and Massachusetts, demonstrated a scientific method for constructing house roofs using projection, rejecting the traditional "cut and try" approach. The family journeyed westward from Ellington, Connecticut, to Lake Ontario and the Black River Country. A letter from Henderson expressed admiration for Angeline, noting her smile resembled hers. The home also had a cherry tree, crab-apple tree, and a hot-bed for winter gardening.

Man, referred to in a poem, has thoughts rich with verdure and perfume, capturing the richness of October and freshness of June; his absence is felt when wild flowers emit an odorous breath. The man is associated with C. A. S. Hall, who on July 14, 1884, prepared breakfast of roast beef, baked potatoes, Graham gems, raspberries and cream, and went to work at Old Brick, Goshen. Samie, now four years old, is well, growing taller and stouter, and has learned most of his letters; he is fond of raspberries and went to the garden to work. Angelo, born September 16, 1868, is described as the nicest little boy, fat and rosy, and has a slight earache but is recovering. Little A, a baby, is bright and smart, and began writing a letter to Sister Mary during vacation, copying her verses. Sister Mary received a letter and tub of apples and cider from Angeline Hall, made apple sauce (never before had boiled cider apple sauce), and intends to repay expenses. The speaker urges the recipient to visit soon, is going with Mary to pick raspberries, and has received two letters from Adelaide, who is expected to leave for Goshen.

Angeline Stickney, a scholar and educator, alternated between teaching and studying, attending seminary in Rodman with her sister Ruth and studying Virgil, Greek, German, natural philosophy, and surveying. She began attending district school at age three, spun flax at five, and by twelve was an excellent housekeeper, sent to help her sister Charlotte Ingalls manage a tavern in Wisconsin. Charlotte, married to Edwin Ingalls, ran a tavern in December 1842 and later prospered in Wisconsin, occasionally bringing the Stickney sisters together. Angeline and Mr. Hall married on Monday morning in Ann Arbor, Michigan, after staying over Sunday at Elder Bright’s, and settled there to pursue studies, planning to remain for three or four years. They lived in Rodman village, where Angeline did family washing on Monday mornings and valued her modest education. The sisters shared board and lodging for one dollar per week, stating they were in the best location for studying domestic economy. Charlotte Ingalls, Edwin Ingalls, and Angeline were all mothers, and the sisters reunited in 1891 near their old home. Edwin Ingalls, known for thrift and character, once calmed fears with a homely rhyme.

Angeline Hall, a devoted mother, performed miracles of healing in her household and rescued the narrator from a hopeless case of dysentery in his fifth year, an event the old Navy doctor called a miracle. She maintained strict health routines, ensuring no boy in her family was late to school for three-year periods. She repaired a missing tooth after Percival’s accident and restored it, which served for twenty years. She borrowed fifty dollars from cousin Joseph Downs to finish her course, repaying him in the following year. Asaph Hall, initially planning to teach in Shalersville, concluded it was unprofitable and preferred carpentry, though he later pursued astronomy at Harvard with encouragement from Professor Brünnow and the Observatory director. His studies were delayed by a storm on Lake Erie, leading to a change in route. The family name "Asaph" was humorously linked to their children’s initials, a notion from the narrator’s boyhood. Sam had a pleasant time with the author reading George Eliot’s Romola, and the author, C. A. S. Hall, expressed love to Sam and planned to visit North Andover with Mrs. Berrien. A. Jr. expressed interest in attending a boat-race and asked when tickets were sold.

Asaph Hall 1st, a Revolutionary War militia captain and chief patriot of Goshen, Connecticut, moved there in 1755, built a house in 1767, and was a friend of Ethan Allen, participating in the capture of Ticonderoga. He served twenty-four times in the State legislature and helped ratify the Federal Constitution. Hall Meadow in Goshen commemorates him. His only child, the second Asaph Hall, born in 1800, was raised as a young gentleman and prepared for Yale College but died in 1842 in Georgia, selling clocks made in his Goshen factory. David Hall, his great-grandfather, was an original proprietor of Goshen and died in battle near Lake George in 1755; his bones lie in an unknown grave nearby. The narrator recalls Asaph Hall, Ethan Allen, and David Hall during a trip to Ticonderoga via steamer, where they saw the old fort and had a farewell view of the mountains. The recipient is advised to pack a dry tent before leaving Keene and take all items from the narrator’s room in Cambridge. Peppermint essence is kept near the west window. C. A. S. HALL traveled through New York and visited Lake Placid, Wilmington Notch, and the Au Sable Chasm before arriving in Ticonderoga.

Moses Stickney, a Revolutionary War veteran, provided a home for his bride Mary Hastings in Jaffrey, New Hampshire, where they lived for sixty-nine years. Mary, descended from an English earl, bore four noble sons and four fair daughters. Moses, a crack shot and five feet ten inches tall, carried a long-barreled musket at Bunker Hill and yoked his oxen at age 100. He owned a farm near Monadnock, now a barren waste marked by raspberry bushes, where Lois and Charlotte, his daughters, died in the fall of 1869. Charlotte, thirteen years older than Angeline Stickney, remembered her father and preserved ancient New Hampshire customs, using expressions like "fiddlesticks" and "witch-cats." Daniel Gilman vexed Moses, who threatened to shoot any young man wooing his daughters. Mary served as a nurse during Little A.'s infancy and nursed him through diphtheria after he got lost and nearly fell into a well. Angeline, Moses’s granddaughter, became deeply interested in family history after visiting her aunts. Perry, a resident of Jaffrey from 1837 to 1847, knew Moses and heard his war stories.

Young Asaph, a sixteen-year-old apprentice in carpentry, served a three-year apprenticeship with Herrick and Dunbar in New Hampshire, receiving board and five dollars a month. He returned to the widow’s house during cold weather to help tend cattle and hunt gray squirrels. He studied geometry and algebra with Mr. Rice of the Norfolk Academy, excelling as a mathematician and solving a problem that baffled students and teachers. After beginning studies at McGrawville, he earned twenty-two dollars a month as a journeyman and gave one hundred dollars to his mother. Young Stickney, a carpenter of twenty-six with curly hair and proven skill, married Electa, daughter of a prosperous farmer, though they did not live happily together. Electa, a dark-haired, rosy-cheeked eighteen-year-old, may have imagined Revolutionary soldiers in three-cornered hats, uniform or homespun, carrying muskets and powder horns. Moses Stickney, a crack shot during the Revolution, carried a long-barreled musket, and stories of his marksmanship are preserved in the Vermont valley. Mt. Monadnock is visible from a high ridge between Vermont valley and the Connecticut River. Angeline Stickney taught school in Heath Hollow and Pleasant Valley, boarding with her sister and spinning wool.

Elisha Cook and Huldah Cook, formerly Huldah Pratt, traveled westward and settled in the wilderness of Black River Country, bringing their children and household goods, using tools like axe, plough, hammer, saw, spinning-wheel, and loom to expand the Kingdom of God. They lived during the War of 1812, when Fort Stanwix echoed with St. Leger’s Indian warwhoops, and Huldah had been in Albany when Burgoyne surrendered. Elisha died in the summer of 1841; Theophilus Stickney died in February 1841 in Rochester, making the Stickney girls orphans. Angeline Stickney, the most knowledgeable about family history, traced her lineage to eleven Englishmen who arrived in New England before 1650 and found her grandfather’s cousin, Thomas Sabin, in 1884, who remembered skating with Elisha Cook. Angeline was undecided between Albany, Oberlin, and McGrawville, ultimately choosing McGrawville where she and her sister lived on one dollar a week. The children suffered from fever and ague; Theophilus returned to the Black River Country to live on the Cook farm after humbling his pride. Matches were not yet in use, and homespun clothing was made with spinning-wheel and loom.

Angeline Stickney, a Puritan woman from New England, instilled strict moral values in her sons, including abstinence from drinking and tobacco, and taught them to believe in woman suffrage while discouraging pride through practical lessons like gathering leaves and covering garments with patches. Despite her strictness, she was deeply sensitive to beauty and nobility, as seen in her exultation over a Maryland sunset viewed with her sons. Her sons suffered from her excess of Puritanism, though their father taught them card playing. Harriette Downes, a graduate of the Young Ladies Institute in Pittsfield, Massachusetts, paid Stickney’s tuition at the Rodman Union Seminary. Stickney believed slavery could be abolished only when men treat others as they wish to be treated, and she held lifelong convictions about slavery shaped by abolitionist influences. She opposed woman suffrage and disapproved of her husband’s poetry, but her maternal love was profound and unmatched.

Nellie, a sensitive and ambitious girl, improved significantly after moving to the household and had many friends; she was buried at Grandfather’s old farm in Rodman after suffering two congestive chills. Her death followed a serious illness in 1881, during which her sister Ruth saved her. Aunt Angeline cared for Nellie when she fell ill and took a lively interest in the family’s welfare. Asaph Hall, a central figure, deeply loves Angie and believes she is holier than he is, expressing that he must undergo trials to be worthy of her. He urges Angie not to hold gloomy thoughts about him, insists on her health and cheerfulness, and expresses strong desire to marry her, expecting to do so in the spring of 1900. He writes to Angie and her mother, affirming trust in their future and a shared hope for a good, happy home. Hall also leaves a note on July 12, 1864, stating he is going to Fort Lincoln under Admiral Goldsborough, and returns to Goshen in December 1856. Angeline, another key figure, experiences a brief paralysis and expresses uncertainty about her future, but Hall remains hopeful and supportive.

Electa Cook, after being impatient toward her first husband, found her impatience avenged in her second marriage, a church ceremony where Mr. Milton Woodward saw her and became interested. The minister suggested the marriage would create a home for her, treating her as if she were not the mistress of seventy-two acres. Electa gave up her independence, possibly sympathizing with the ten motherless Woodward children or loving Mr. Woodward, who had a violent temper and abused her. He opposed her bringing her unmarried daughters to his house, though two of them later married step-brothers and shared the Woodward fate. The marriage occurred during a cold season with snow on the ground and a noisy, Sabbath-less church. Angeline, upon learning of her mother’s marriage, quoted from *The Lady of the Lake*, a line deemed appropriate for the situation. She lived as a white slave in the family of wrangling siblings and threatened to rescue her mother by carrying her to Cambridge.

The hero liberated Hesione from chains and freed an arm from a sea-monster, prevailing over Death while standing near with a heart that never faltered; the gods granted her a shining panoply after she chose virtue over Vice. Nature obeyed her will, causing rivers to rush from their ancient beds and wash the earth’s filth into the sea. When her arrows were exhausted, Zeus sent stones in a snow-cloud and Helios provided a golden boat to carry her safely across the sea. A poet, associated with POEM, expressed deep faith in science as a force of truth and freedom, describing it as invulnerable and victorious against enemies, with clouds praised for their beauty and forms in sunlight and storms. Jasper Woodward, a lieutenant and the best of the Woodward brothers, led his company at Bull Run, gloried in battle, and died after taking cold in a damp stone church following a retreat; Constant, his step-brother, took a last shot in revenge and was wounded.

She was a woman of strong spiritual force, with beautiful brown eyes, thin curls of fine dark hair, and a well-developed frame due to her refusal of corsets. She possessed a high-order intellect, excellent mathematical ability, and a strong sense of duty, dedicating her talents to serving others. Though physically bent from years of toil and lacking nervous strength, she endured childbirth with unusual fortitude and performed the work of two women through sheer will. She died at sixty-two from a stroke due to worn-out brain blood vessels. Friends and relatives regarded her as a wise counsellor and fearless leader. She had a more fortunate marriage than her friend’s, converting her pagan partner, though the Unitarian Church eventually became too narrow for her. Mr. Pritchett, an astronomer clergyman from Missouri, donated to her husband and was the father of Dr. Henry S. Pritchett, who later became a member of the Hall family after receiving assistance from Mr. Hall during his studies.

Asaph Hall, Jr. was born at the Bond Cottage on October 6, 1859, and showed early precocity, playing bo-peep at four months, weighing 21 pounds at six months, and beginning housework at two and a half years, declaring "I’m big enough, mama." The Halls lived in the Bond Cottage on Observatory Hill in Cambridge from 1859 to 1862, where they practiced division of labor, which Asaph claimed stemmed from small family disagreements and led to greater household harmony and success. Angeline, who worked at the Woodward farm until 1847, performed extensive housework, including baking and milking cows, and was known for her academic abilities in grammar and arithmetic. A dull boy from Rodman found arithmetic perplexing but admired Miss Stickney, who carefully explained it, considering her his ideal woman. The cottage had a vegetable garden that raised delicious sweet corn during its growing season. Woodward children ridiculed Angeline, calling her "Lady Angeline," a title she lived up to.

Mrs. Asaph Hall, also known as Angeline S. Hall, was a self-reliant and principled woman who supported social reform, such as the abolition of skirts in favor of bloomers, though she and the ladies were not in favor of wearing them themselves. She was furious at her husband’s opposition, calling him a coward and believing a pure-minded woman should not be interfered with. After Asaph Hall entered permanent government service in Washington, she took charge of family affairs, allowing him to focus on science. She walked to school each morning at her aunt Clary Downs’s, a mile and a half from the seminary, enduring harsh winter conditions that caused her to catch a severe cold. One night, she watched Asaph Hall brave a blazing lamp, praising his courage—something he had not noticed before. A family quarrel led her to withdraw from the Unitarian Sunday School, after which she assumed full responsibility for teaching her sons Christian morals. Asaph Hall later acknowledged the quality of his wife, saying it took him a long time to realize what a good wife he had.

Central College is described as welcoming people of every language and race, offering knowledge in crystal brightness, and embodying a form of fanaticism the narrator embraces. It is often seen glowing with golden light, especially at sunrise, symbolizing a sun of truth that drives error away. Angeline Stickney, a former student, bid farewell to her fellow students and took a lingering look at the college, which she found more beautiful than ever. She wrote verses in October 1847 describing leaving a grove, autumnal breezes, falling leaves, and a hope to return in spring when birds sing and wild flowers bloom. E. A. Bulfinch read her verses, which reflected her personality and were described as beautiful and authentic, and felt an emotional connection, imagining seeing her. A high mountain with a castle of green ivy and limestone serves as a guide for sailors, a garden of green with the fairest flowers, suitable for hunting, fishing, and fowling. Asaph Hall hunted wild flowers with his frail wife. Ships from the East Indies travel westward with red flags, drums, and guns, accompanied by sweet music.

The Earth turns on its axis and orbits a vast circle, appearing as a small speck compared to God’s works; its form, weight, and motion are studied, and humans are encouraged to explore the solar system and beyond, where star-gems—vast suns in harmony and beauty—reflect God’s greatness, excellence, majesty, awe, reverence, and love. Our world is described as beautiful, filled with flowers, forests, fields, birds, murmuring brooks, rainbows, and a clear blue sky, containing enough beauty to feast the eyes. Beauty and sublimity are pursued through different paths: one worships Beauty as an ideal, the other lays hold on sublimity in rapture; both seek the spiritual, forming a perfect crystal centered on Truth through the harmony of brain and heart. Knowledge, virtue, and truth are equally accessible to men and women, with any aid benefiting both. Religious tolerance is justified, with moral and human principles preceding specific denominations. Science is portrayed as a path to Truth, guiding beyond the sun and celestial music, while also being a friend to Faith, driving her from idealized realms into wider, real discoveries.

C. A. STICKNEY opposes a detestable law that undermines free institutions, calling it tyranny and injustice, and argues that dissolving the union would not harm the North or South, as it would end slavery and allow the South to learn repentance. She asserts that robbing a man of liberty is the worst form of robbery and foulest form of piracy, and condemns a law that pays commissioners ten dollars for enslaving a fugitive and five for freeing one, calling it legislative bribery and the basest iniquity. The law of God (Deut. 23:15–16) prohibits returning a runaway slave to his master and allows the escaped servant to dwell among the people. Slavery is depicted as cruel, with slaves half-clothed, half-starved, whipped, and driven away from home. Freedom is equally valued by masters and slaves, both having fought for it with ancestors led by Washington. Angeline Hall, aided by Moses, resists the law and receives money from poet Lowell. Many advocate for the slave, though some still hold slaves. Cruelties involving slavery are expected to cease.

Angeline Hall, a Puritan maiden with a strong imitative nature, developed her style through continuous adjustments and successive mixtures, shaped by her love for the beautiful in others, contrasting with Angeline’s lack of imitativeness and singular emergence under the Spirit of the Beautiful. She attended a convention in Saratoga on Wednesday, staying until the afternoon of the next day, where she observed fashionable women displaying their dresses as "gilded butterflies" with no purpose beyond show, contrasting with the earnest working women who spoke about awakening to usefulness. A letter to Mr. Hall, written on Wednesday after the afternoon, expressed her disapproval of feminine adornment, including the use of carbolic acid while washing lamp-chimneys. Despite Puritan opposition, Mr. Hall obtained an engagement ring, which was filed apart by her astronomer husband but worn faithfully for twenty years. Angeline showed consistent sympathy for her mother and sisters, with little contact to her family.

Mountains symbolize Christian aspirations, embodying majesty, steadfastness, and peace that transcends sheltered valleys, rising heavenward with broad bases spreading love and sweet waters. The Christian soul must endure trials—earthquake shocks, red fires, and agonizing suffering—to rise and achieve peace through victory in the calm heavens, where Christ’s sacrifice wins eternal form and unshaken foundations. These trials lift the soul into Heaven of perfect peace, where it works as sovereign energy. Angeline Hall, loving astronomy and hoping for peace, published verses celebrating Donati’s comet as a visible spirit with burning stars and robes of light, gliding through silent space, urging open gates to heaven. A speaker on June 3rd feels ill, fearing consumption and unworthiness, praying for cleansing in Christ’s blood and desiring a name in the Lamb’s Book of Life rather than fame. Love-scenes, tender and ardent, are known only in heaven, where the beloved’s white plumes and angelic wings are seen. A person is urged to offer youth to God instead of worshiping Fame.

The study of astronomy provides exalted views of the Creator, elevates the human soul, binds it to the soul of the Infinite, and reveals great wonders. Lydia, whose name signifies playful or sportive, possesses a vivid, active imagination marked by fiery, sparkling thoughts that fly among the stars, turning, diving, and wondering, with laughter that wells up internally and is laced with sarcasm and drollness; she laughs at funny things and dreams of jokes and quips. Angeline, in contrast, has a gradually glowing imagination like a blowing rose, uses speech utilitarianistically, and only laughs when someone is present to talk about fun; her laughter comes from outside her face, like pale moonlight, and she laughs about rather than at humor. The speaker believes quoting verses is a betrayal because the person produced better poetry, citing examples of deep friendship, longing to be remembered, and love for life, with ten thousand cords binding the soul to existence and sweet looks and tones winning the heart, as nature grows more beautiful each year.

Mary Gilman, daughter of Mrs. Hall’s cousin, married Lyman, who began haying but had his hay affected by rain on Friday and Saturday afternoons. Lyman will take over the Torrington creamery, which will disappoint Mary, who is trying to secure a fixed salary and hopes the speaker will succeed. No salary arrangements were made for the creamery position. Mary was once a student at McGrawville and came to Shalersville to enlarge the institute’s curriculum in fine arts, though she hindered more than she helped and left in January after teaching Angeline to paint in oil. Lyman, married to Mary, has no salary arrangements for his new role. At the Harvard Observatory, Asaph Hall received only $3 per week initially, later advanced to $4, while Mr. Hall earned $600 annually but saved $300 due to frugality, accepting $1,000 in paper money (equivalent to $800 in gold) from the Bonds despite the war’s uncertainties and Washington’s poor conditions.

The woman, described as possessing subtle, penetrating sweetness and living a spiritual life rooted in unselfishness and charity, uplifted the poor and transformed their degraded ideal of human life through acts of kindness drawn from her own need, not surplus. She welcomed all for their humanity, offering hospitality as sacred as a hearth altar, and lived with humility akin to a child. Her life reflected a higher range of being, marked by stillness, purity, and deep belief in God, the soul, and the spirit of Christ. She rejected social boundaries, embraced the good in every soul—even when mixed with evil—seeing it as divine, and avoided harm through witticism. She believed suffering humanity needed noble spirits and sought to cultivate such qualities in others, as seen in her encouragement of Ruth to pursue education and join reform. The child, named Chloe Angeline—a name borrowed from a cheap novel—may have been protected from silly women and blessed with strength; her birth was not attended by all saints, and her spirit was said to be revealed as Christ’s through a legend akin to St. Christopher, who bore a child safely across waters, symbolizing divine protection and sacrifice. Earth’s angels are described as noble souls who give their lives to perishing and oppressed humanity.

Lydia and Angeline are both skilled in prose and poetic composition, with Lydia being more renowned and exhibiting a naturally ambitious, quiet, and complacent disposition. Lydia’s work reveals both poet and artist, marked by ornamental style and a Calvinistic influence characterized by election and predestination, while Angeline’s writings show only the poet, lacking prior knowledge of style and hindered by scientific studies. Lydia is more artificial and artistic than Angeline, whose ambition develops slowly from moral desires and friendly encouragement. Angeline lives in Jefferson County, where the skies are as clear as in Italy, and she finds beauty and grandeur in nature, inspired by her childhood. The narrator, born in September 1868, once twined the graces of violet, anemone, hepatica, and arbutus, laying a garland at a poet’s feet. Violet is described as dreaming of the sky and awakening with heaven’s azure in her eye and fragrance in her air. Mrs. Hall witnessed veterans, including General Osborne from Jefferson County, whose battle-flags were torn but arms burnished, admired as the finest soldiers. The speaker apologizes for quoting the poetess, noting she produced better poetry elsewhere.

The timid woman, Mrs. Hall, cultivated a vibrant garden where each son had a dedicated rose-bush—one for her husband and one for his mother. Her garden featured diverse flora, including lilies of the valley in the shady yard, gladiolas, Easter lilies, and other lilies scattered throughout, with crocuses, hyacinths, and daffodils in early spring. Vines, especially English ivy, trailed along fences and climbed house sides, while honeysuckles, hollyhocks, morning-glories, sweet-briar roses, wisterias, a magnolia near the parlor window, forsythia by the front fence, and a flowering bush by the side alley added to the beauty. Flower beds, bordered by walks, hosted roses, petunias, verbenas, geraniums, portulacas, and mignonnette, attracting hummingbirds. The yard was fenced with iron pickets made from old gun barrels, giving the property the name "Gunbarrel Corner." Mrs. Hall brought wild flowers from the woods behind Georgetown into her yard, using rich wood’s earth from a decaying old tree. Uncle Louis, aged 114, rewarded her with a grape-vine planted by the dining room window, which produced the best grapes in the garden, known as the Uncle Louis grape.
